target: Eu arrumo a cama logo que acordo.
english: I make the bed as soon as I wake up.
tip: 'Logo que' + present tense means 'as soon as.' It's very common in daily Brazilian Portuguese.

target: A gente aluga uma casa na praia no verão.
english: We rent a house at the beach in the summer.
tip: a gente means 'we' but takes the he/she verb form: a gente aluga, not alugamos.

target: O tempo está bom hoje para ir à praia.
english: The weather is nice today to go to the beach.
tip: Weather and temperature use 'estar' because they change – 'O tempo está bom' (the weather is good right now).

target: Ele foi ao mercado comprar coisas para o jantar.
english: He went to the market to buy things for dinner.
tip: After a motion verb, a bare infinitive shows purpose, with no 'para' needed: 'foi ao mercado comprar' = went to buy.

target: Eu acordo às cinco e meia para ir à academia.
english: I wake up at 5:30 to go to the gym.
tip: 'À academia' uses the contraction 'à' (a + a) because 'academia' is feminine and 'ir a' requires the preposition 'a.'

target: Eu passo no mercado na volta do trabalho.
english: I stop by the store on the way back from work.
tip: 'Passar em' means to stop by or drop by a place. It's one of the most common uses of 'passar' in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
Masculine plural covers mixed groups: 'irmãos' means brothers, or siblings of both genders. An all-female set would be 'irmãs.'
Quem (who) as a subject always takes a singular verb: quem cozinhou, even if more than one person might have cooked.
estar plus an -ndo verb makes the present continuous: estou aprendendo is 'I'm learning', an action underway right now.
'Simpática' means nice or friendly, not 'sympathetic.' It describes a warm, likeable person.
'A gente' means 'we' but takes a singular verb: 'a gente é,' never 'a gente somos.' It is the everyday spoken 'we.'

english: I have a pain in my back.
tip: Portuguese uses 'estar com' + noun where English uses 'to be' + adjective: 'estou com fome' (I'm hungry), 'estou com frio' (I'm cold).

target: Nós estamos com saudade de casa.
tip: 'Saudade' is a uniquely Portuguese word for a deep longing or missing. 'Estar com saudade de' is how you express missing someone or something.

target: A água do mar é salgada.
tip: Inherent traits take ser: a água do mar é salgada. Salt is part of what seawater is, not a passing state.
'Ser' for origin: 'vocês são de onde?' Word order is flexible in questions – 'de onde vocês são?' also works.
No article before a profession: 'ele é engenheiro,' not 'um engenheiro.' Portuguese drops the 'a/an' that English uses here.
For where a place is, Brazilians use ficar: Onde fica o banheiro means 'where is the bathroom', with ficar marking a settled location.
dar aulas, literally 'to give classes', means to teach: dou aulas de português is 'I teach Portuguese'.
'Ser' + 'de' for origin: 'nós somos de Belo Horizonte.' This is permanent identity, so use 'ser.'
'Ter medo de' means 'to be afraid of' – literally 'to have fear of.' Many English 'be' expressions use 'ter' in Portuguese.
Portuguese has an allergy rather than being allergic: tenho alergia a camarão = I'm allergic to shrimp.
estar plus a gerund is English '-ing' in progress: estamos planejando means 'we are planning'. Brazilians lean on it constantly.
Traffic conditions change daily – use 'estar.' If you said 'o trânsito é horrível,' you'd mean it's always terrible.
Comparatives just add 'mais' before the adjective: 'mais barato' = cheaper. No word ending changes.

target: A gente pode ir a pé.
tip: 'Ir a pé,' literally 'go by foot,' means to walk somewhere: 'a gente pode ir a pé.'

target: Qual é o seu número de telefone?
tip: Portuguese asks Qual é, not O que, for numbers and names: Qual é o seu número. It is 'which is' where English says 'what'.
'Fazer aniversário,' literally 'to make a birthday,' is how you say to have a birthday: 'faço aniversário em março.'
Days of the week take 'no/na' for 'on': 'no sábado' = on Saturday. There is no separate word for 'on.'
Emotion adjectives take com for the thing that caused them: surpreso com a notícia (surprised by the news), where English uses by or at.
The room can be cleaned – the mess is a temporary state, so use 'estar.' If you said 'é uma bagunça,' you'd mean it's inherently messy.
